Here, we bring hybrid parametric and non-parametric memory to the “workhorse of NLP,” i.e. sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models. We endow pre-trained, parametric-memory generation models with a non-parametric memory through a general-purpose fine-tuning approach which we refer to as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We build RAG models where the parametric memory is a pre-trained seq2seq transformer, and the non-parametric memory is a dense vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever. We combine these components in a probabilistic model trained end-to-end (Fig.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: vector index of Wikipedia, accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever. We combine these components in a probabilistic model trained end-to-end (Fig. 1). The retriever (Dense Passage Retriever [26], henceforth DPR) provides latent documents conditioned on the input, and the seq2seq model (BART [32]) then conditions on these latent documents together with the input to generate the output. We marginalize the latent documents with a top-K approximation, either on a per-output basis (assuming the same document is responsible for all tokens) or a per-token basis (where different documents are responsible for different tokens). Like T5 [51] or BART, RAG can be fine-tuned on any seq2seq task, whereby both the generator and retriever are jointly learned. There has been extensive previous work proposing architectures to enrich systems with non-parametric memory which are trained from scratch for

There has been extensive previous work proposing architectures to enrich systems with non-parametric memory which are trained from scratch for specific tasks, e.g. memory networks [64, 55], stackaugmented networks [25] and memory layers [30]. In contrast, we explore a setting where both parametric and non-parametric memory components are pre-trained and pre-loaded with extensive knowledge. Crucially, by using pre-trained access mechanisms, the ability to access knowledge is present without additional training. Our results highlight the benefits of combining parametric and non-parametric memory with generation for knowledge-intensive tasks—tasks that humans could not reasonably be expected to perform without access to an external knowledge source. Our RAG models achieve state-of-the-art results on open Natural Questions [29], WebQuestions [3] and CuratedTrec [2] and strongly outperform

Our RAG models achieve state-of-the-art results on open Natural Questions [29], WebQuestions [3] and CuratedTrec [2] and strongly outperform recent approaches that use specialised pre-training objectives on TriviaQA [24]. Despite these being extractive tasks, we find that unconstrained generation outperforms previous extractive approaches. For knowledge-intensive generation, we experiment with MS-MARCO [1] and Jeopardy question generation, and we find that our models generate responses that are more factual, specific, and diverse than a BART baseline. For FEVER [56] fact verification, we achieve results within 4.3% of state-of-the-art pipeline models which use strong retrieval supervision. For all experiments, we use a single Wikipedia dump for our non-parametric knowledge source. Following Lee et al. [31] and Karpukhin et al. [26], we use the December 2018 dump. We now discuss experimental details for each task. 3.1 Open-domain Question Answering Open-domain question answering (QA) is an important real-world application and common testbed for knowledge-intensive tasks [20]. We treat questions and answers as input-output text pairs (x, y) and train RAG by directly minimizing the negative log-likelihood of answers. We compare RAG to the popular extractive QA paradigm [5, 7, 31, 26], where answers are extracted spans from retrieved documents, relying primarily on non-parametric knowledge. We also compare to “Closed-Book QA” approaches [52], which, like RAG, generate answers, but which do not exploit retrieval, instead relying purely on parametric knowledge. We consider four popular open-domain QA datasets: Natural Questions (NQ) [29], TriviaQA (TQA) [24]. WebQuestions (WQ) [3] and CuratedTrec (CT) [2]. As CT and WQ are small, we follow DPR [26] by initializing CT and WQ models with our NQ RAG model. We use the same train/dev/test splits as prior work [31, 26] and report Exact Match (EM) scores. Rather than use questions from standard open-domain QA tasks, which typically consist of short, simple questions, we propose the more demanding task of generating Jeopardy questions. For example, “The World Cup” is the answer to the question “In 1986 Mexico scored as the first country to host this international sports competition twice.” As Jeopardy questions are precise, factual statements, generating Jeopardy questions conditioned on their answer entities constitutes a challenging knowledge-intensive generation task. We use the splits from SearchQA [10], with 100K train, 14K dev, and 27K test examples. As this is a new task, we train a BART model for comparison. Following [67], we evaluate using the SQuAD-tuned Q-BLEU-1 metric [42]. Q-BLEU is a variant of BLEU with a higher weight for matching entities and has higher correlation with human judgment for question generation than standard metrics. We follow best practice and use pairwise comparative evaluation [34]. Evaluators are shown an answer and two generated questions, one from BART and one from RAG. To assess the effectiveness of the retrieval mechanism, we run ablations where we freeze the retriever during training. As shown in Table 6, learned retrieval improves results for all tasks. We compare RAG's dense retriever to a word overlap-based BM25 retriever [53]. Here, we replace RAG's retriever with a fixed BM25 system, and use BM25 retrieval scores as logits when calculating p(z|x). Table 6 show the results. For FEVER, BM25 performs best, perhaps since FEVER claims are heavily entity-centric and thus well-suited for word overlap-based retrieval. Index hot-swapping An advantage of non-parametric memory models like RAG is that knowledge can be easily updated at test time. Parametric-only models like T5 or BART need further training to update their behavior as the world changes. To demonstrate, we build an index using the DrQA [5] Wikipedia dump from December 2016 and compare outputs from RAG using this index to the newer index from our main results (December 2018). Right: MS-MARCO Bleu-1 and Rouge-L as more documents are retrieved. 5 Related Work Single-Task Retrieval Prior work has shown that retrieval improves performance across a variety of NLP tasks when considered in isolation. Such tasks include open-domain question answering [5, 29], fact checking [56], fact completion [48], long-form question answering [12], Wikipedia article generation [36], dialogue [41, 65, 9, 13], translation [17], and language modeling [19, 27]. Our work unifies previous successes in incorporating retrieval into individual tasks, showing that a single retrieval-based architecture is capable of achieving strong performance across several tasks.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: General-Purpose Architectures for NLP Prior work on general-purpose architectures for NLP tasks has shown great success without the use of retrieval. A single, pre-trained language model has been shown to achieve strong performance on various classification tasks in the GLUE benchmarks [60, 61] after fine-tuning [49, 8]. GPT-2 [50] later showed that a single, left-to-right, pre-trained language model could achieve strong performance across both discriminative and generative tasks. For further improvement, BART [32] and T5 [51, 52] propose a single, pre-trained encoder-decoder model that leverages bi-directional attention to achieve stronger performance on discriminative and generative tasks. Our work aims to expand the space of possible tasks with a single, unified architecture, by learning a retrieval module to augment pre-trained, generative language models. Learned Retrieval There is

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: tasks with a single, unified architecture, by learning a retrieval module to augment pre-trained, generative language models. Learned Retrieval There is significant work on learning to retrieve documents in information retrieval, more recently with pre-trained, neural language models [44, 26] similar to ours. Some work optimizes the retrieval module to aid in a specific, downstream task such as question answering, using search [46], reinforcement learning [6, 63, 62], or a latent variable approach [31, 20] as in our work. These successes leverage different retrieval-based architectures and optimization techniques to achieve strong performance on a single task, while we show that a single retrieval-based architecture can be fine-tuned for strong performance on a variety of tasks. Memory-based Architectures Our document index can be seen as a large external memory for neural networks to attend

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: performance on a variety of tasks. Memory-based Architectures Our document index can be seen as a large external memory for neural networks to attend to, analogous to memory networks [64, 55]. Concurrent work [14] learns to retrieve a trained embedding for each entity in the input, rather than to retrieve raw text as in our work. Other work improves the ability of dialog models to generate factual text by attending over fact embeddings [9, 13] or, closer to our work, over retrieved text directly [15]. A key feature of our memory is that it is comprised of raw text rather distributed representations, which makes the memory both (i) human-readable, lending a form of interpretability to our model, and (ii) human-writable, enabling us to dynamically update the model's memory by editing the document index. Retrieve-and-Edit approaches Our method shares some similarities with retrieve-and-edit

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: dynamically update the model's memory by editing the document index. Retrieve-and-Edit approaches Our method shares some similarities with retrieve-and-edit style approaches, where a similar training input-output pair is retrieved for a given input, and then edited to provide a final output. These approaches have proved successful in a number of domains including Machine Translation [18, 22] and Semantic Parsing [21]. Our approach does have several differences, including less of emphasis on lightly editing a retrieved item, but on aggregating content from several pieces of retrieved content, as well as learning latent retrieval, and retrieving evidence documents rather than related training pairs. This said, RAG techniques may work well in these settings, and could represent promising future work. 6 Discussion In this work, we presented hybrid generation models with access to parametric

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: these settings, and could represent promising future work. 6 Discussion In this work, we presented hybrid generation models with access to parametric and non-parametric memory. We showed that our RAG models obtain state of the art results on open-domain QA. We found that people prefer RAG's generation over purely parametric BART, finding RAG more factual and specific. We conducted an thorough investigation of the learned retrieval component, validating its effectiveness, and we illustrated how the retrieval index can be hot-swapped to update the model without requiring any retraining. In future work, it may be fruitful to investigate if the two components can be jointly pre-trained from scratch, either with a denoising objective similar to BART or some another objective. Our work opens up new research directions on how parametric and non-parametric memories interact and how to most effectively

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: or some another objective. Our work opens up new research directions on how parametric and non-parametric memories interact and how to most effectively combine them, showing promise in being applied to a wide variety of NLP tasks.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: Broader Impact This work offers several positive societal benefits over previous work: the fact that it is more strongly grounded in real factual knowledge (in this case Wikipedia) makes it “hallucinate” less with generations that are more factual, and offers more control and interpretability. RAG could be employed in a wide variety of scenarios with direct benefit to society, for example by endowing it with a medical index and asking it open-domain questions on that topic, or by helping people be more effective at their jobs. With these advantages also come potential downsides: Wikipedia, or any potential external knowledge source, will probably never be entirely factual and completely devoid of bias. Since RAG can be employed as a language model, similar concerns as for GPT-2 [50] are valid here, although arguably to a lesser extent, including that it might be used to generate abuse, faked

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: model, similar concerns as for GPT-2 [50] are valid here, although arguably to a lesser extent, including that it might be used to generate abuse, faked or misleading content in the news or on social media; to impersonate others; or to automate the production of spam/phishing content [54]. Advanced language models may also lead to the automation of various jobs in the coming decades [16]. In order to mitigate these risks, AI systems could be employed to fight against misleading content and automated spam/phishing. title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation Abstract In recent years, the continuous advancement of large language models (LLMs) has driven the development of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC). To address issues such as hallucinations in AIGC, the inability to provide accurate real-time information, or the failure to answer domain-specific questions, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), proposed in the last two years, has effectively solved a series of problems by enabling LLMs to access external knowledge sources and integrating retrieved content with LLMs. This paper first reviews the development and advantages of RAG, such as providing real-time and accurate information, enhancing the capabilities of LLMs, and improving the credibility and transparency of output results. It then introduces the architecture of RAG systems, including retrievers, generators,

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: and improving the credibility and transparency of output results. It then introduces the architecture of RAG systems, including retrievers, generators, language models, and their relationships. Furthermore, it presents different RAG tools for various problems, such as SelfRAG, GraphRAG, and RankRAG. By analyzing research data, the paper summarizes the applicable scenarios of these three RAG technologies: SelfRAG improves factuality and citation accuracy by approximately 80% compared to traditional RAG, performing the best; GraphRAG excels in handling large-scale complex data, with a diversity advantage exceeding 62%; and RankRAG demonstrates outstanding efficiency in ranking-related tasks, with a 10% improvement in reasoning performance and a reduction in time cost to one-sixth of the original. Additionally, based on the existing problems and limitations of RAG systems, as well as some current

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: reduction in time cost to one-sixth of the original. Additionally, based on the existing problems and limitations of RAG systems, as well as some current model analysis methods, the paper discusses future trends in RAG, including improving efficiency, expanding application scope, multimodal processing, and hybrid approaches. Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Large Language Models (LLM), Information Retrieval, Chatbot, Generative Models, Ranking Models, Knowledge Graph Contribution： This paper addresses the issue that current RAG survey writers often focus on introducing various state-of-the-art RAG research and development technologies but lack explanations on how and when to use RAG. The paper provides a detailed introduction to RAG technology, covering its origins, working principles, basic framework, and the problems RAG can solve. Much of the foundational content about

Much of the foundational content about RAG is not covered in previous surveys. This paper can better help everyone quickly understand this revolutionary technology. At the same time, the paper focuses on analyzing three retrieval methods: SelfRAG, GraphRAG, and RankRAG. By comparing the specific data of these technologies on certain benchmarks with traditional large language models or conventional RAG, it clarifies the scenarios each technology is suited for, helping readers quickly choose the technique they need. title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: Research Objective: In recent years, the rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has driven advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and AI-generated content (AIGC). However, traditional LLMs suffer from issues such as a lack of timeliness and domain-specific expertise, which has led to the emergence of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) technology. RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation, which involves prompting a large language model (LLM) to access specific data sources, retrieve relevant information, and generate answers based on that retrieved content. The concept of RAG originated from information retrieval and natural language processing (NLP). The term was first introduced in a 2020 paper titled "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" by Patrick Lewis et al. This paper presented a novel approach that combined a pre-trained retriever

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" by Patrick Lewis et al. This paper presented a novel approach that combined a pre-trained retriever with a seq2seq model to enhance the knowledge capabilities of LLM-based systems. This research marked the birth of the RAG concept and laid the foundation for its future development. At this stage, RAG's primary purpose was to strengthen the reasoning abilities of LLMs through foundational pre-training, ensuring they could access and accurately manipulate knowledge in knowledge-intensive tasks (Lewis,P et al.2020,Borgeaud,S et al,2021). RAG has been widely applied in downstream NLP tasks. By retrieving textual information, RAG enables functions such as summarization, dialogue generation, and knowledge-intensive generation(Lewis,P et al.2020, Izacard, G, et al,2020). Since Google introduced the transformer model in its 2017

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: generation, and knowledge-intensive generation(Lewis,P et al.2020, Izacard, G, et al,2020). Since Google introduced the transformer model in its 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need," the field of artificial intelligence has undergone significant changes. Google subsequently released BERT (a bidirectional transformer model) in 2018 and AlphaFold in 2021, greatly enhancing LLMs' ability to understand context in natural language processing. However, these models did not perform satisfactorily when applied to RAG. It wasn't until November 2022, when OpenAI launched ChatGPT, that the landscape changed entirely. Based on the GPT architecture, ChatGPT can understand and generate natural language, making it suitable for tasks such as conversation, question answering, and text generation. Through reinforcement learning and human feedback, ChatGPT can provide coherent and meaningful responses in

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: conversation, question answering, and text generation. Through reinforcement learning and human feedback, ChatGPT can provide coherent and meaningful responses in dialogues (Ouyang, L et al,2022). Its ability to handle follow-up questions, admit mistakes, challenge incorrect human queries, and reject inappropriate requests has made it immensely popular, elevating ChatGPT to heights unmatched by other LLMs. Since then, the long-context learning capabilities of LLMs have significantly improved, and RAG's role has expanded beyond reasoning to become integrated into the fine-tuning and generation processes of LLMs, yielding positive results. The rise of LLMs has made RAG increasingly popular in NLP tasks (Achiam, O.J et al,2022). The core idea of RAG is to enable LLMs to leverage external knowledge sources when generating responses. Based on its primary architecture, the process can be divided

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: RAG is to enable LLMs to leverage external knowledge sources when generating responses. Based on its primary architecture, the process can be divided into two parts: data preparation and retrieval-generation. This represents the earliest approach under the Naive RAG research paradigm, which gained prominence shortly after the widespread adoption of ChatGPT. Naive RAG follows a conventional process consisting of indexing, retrieval, and generation, also described as the "retrieve-then-read" framework (X. Ma et al,2023). The defining feature of RAG lies in its introduction of an information retrieval component. This preprint research paper has not been peer reviewed. title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: When a user submits a query, this component extracts relevant information from external data sources. The retrieved information, along with the user query, is then fed into the LLM, which synthesizes this new knowledge with its original training data to produce more accurate and contextually relevant responses. External data can originate from APIs, databases, or document repositories and is converted into a digital format using AI techniques to create a knowledge base that the LLM can comprehend. However, traditional RAG systems still face various challenges. To address these issues, three retrieval methods—SelfRAG, GraphRAG, and RankRAG—have emerged, leveraging selfreflection, cognitive graph construction, and relevance ranking techniques, respectively, to overcome a series of limitations. These innovations have opened a new chapter in the development of RAG technology. 1. Working Principle

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: respectively, to overcome a series of limitations. These innovations have opened a new chapter in the development of RAG technology. 1. Working Principle and Architecture of RAG 1.1 Data Preparation Data preparation is a critical phase. This process involves data extraction, context-aware data annotation, document chunking, vector embedding conversion, and database storage. 1.1.1 Data Extraction This step involves consolidating data obtained from various online formats (e.g., TXT, PDF, Markdown) into a unified format. Synonyms and diverse expressions are standardized to facilitate efficient retrieval by the model. 1.1.2 Context Processing and Chunking Coherent text is divided into chunks of a certain size, which could range from partial sentences to full paragraphs. Multiple text splitters are available for this task, with the most common method being segmentation into fixed token counts

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: sentences to full paragraphs. Multiple text splitters are available for this task, with the most common method being segmentation into fixed token counts (e.g., 100, 256, or 512 tokens) (R.Teja,2024). However, this approach struggles to balance text length and semantic coherence. To address this, the Child-Parent Recursive Retriever method was proposed. Here, retrieval generates both small ("child") chunks and larger ("parent") chunks. The child chunks (e.g., sentences) serve as retrieval units, while the parent chunks (child chunks plus their surrounding context) provide broader context to the LLM (S.Yang,2024). Properly configuring chunk sizes significantly enhances the LLM's semantic understanding of the text and aids in relevance ranking (e.g., top-k retrieval). 1.1.3 Vector Embedding and Database Storage Vector embedding is a technique for converting words, sentences, and other data

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: ranking (e.g., top-k retrieval). 1.1.3 Vector Embedding and Database Storage Vector embedding is a technique for converting words, sentences, and other data into numerical representations to measure the relevance of text strings. By representing different data types as points in a multidimensional space, similar data points are positioned closer together, enabling machines to understand and process the data more efficiently. This preprint research paper has not been peer reviewed. Electronic copy available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5252835

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: State-of-the-art embedding models like AngIE, Voyage, and BGE (X. Li& J. Li,2023, VoyageAI,2024, BAAI,2023) can transform complex unstructured data (e.g., text, audio, video) into vectors—coordinates in a multidimensional space. Vector representation allows batch operations on dataset elements rather than individual processing and helps LLMs ignore ambiguous words or meaningless particles, enabling effective semantic search. Finally, data with similar semantic or structural features are grouped and stored in a vector database, which is specifically designed to handle and organize large-scale unstructured data. By computing similarity or distance between vector chunks, the database enables rapid localization and retrieval of relevant data. 1.2 Retrieval 1.2.1 Influencing Factors Data Structure: Initially, the retrieval sources were mainly unstructured text, which later expanded to include

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: 1.2 Retrieval 1.2.1 Influencing Factors Data Structure: Initially, the retrieval sources were mainly unstructured text, which later expanded to include structured data such as knowledge graphs and tables, enhancing the retrieval capabilities of LLMs. Unstructured data, such as text, remains the most widely used retrieval source. The primary application domain of RAG is still open-domain question answering, with main data sources including encyclopedias and domain-specific data such as medical and legal fields (Gao Y et al, 2023, S.-Q. Yan, et al,2024). Semi-structured data, such as JSON and XML, have flexible structures but do not conform to tabular data models or relational database formats. Typically, only partially analyzable structured elements are present, making it difficult for current RAG systems to effectively retrieve all content from them. Structured Data: To enhance knowledge-based

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: elements are present, making it difficult for current RAG systems to effectively retrieve all content from them. Structured Data: To enhance knowledge-based question answering, structured data such as knowledge graphs (KGs) (Gaur, M.et al,2021)and tables have been introduced to help LLMs obtain more precise information. For example, the ODQA framework converts KGs into natural language (Ma, K.et al,2022), while Heterformer embeds graphs into each transformer layer to retrieve question-relevant content (Jin, B.et al,2022). CLTR (Pan, F.et al,2021) and FeTaQA (Nan, L.et al,2021) propose transformer-based methods for retrieving the most relevant tables and identifying correct cells, along with novel datasets for interactive questions (e.g., "why"-type queries) and corresponding free-form answers. 1.2.2 Retrieval Granularity Retrieval granularity refers to the size of text chunks during processing.

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: "why"-type queries) and corresponding free-form answers. 1.2.2 Retrieval Granularity Retrieval granularity refers to the size of text chunks during processing. In text retrieval, granularity ranges from fine to coarse, including tokens, phrases, sentences, propositions, chunks, and full documents. Among these, DenseX uses the concept of "propositions" (T. Chen et al,2023) to segment text. A proposition is a refined statement that accurately and completely expresses atomic facts in the text, presented in a concise and self-contained natural language form. This approach effectively balances the issues of overly coarse granularity (which may include redundant information and distract the retriever and language model in downstream tasks (Shi, F.et al,2023)) and overly fine granularity (which may compromise semantic integrity). The retrieval system uses algorithms (such as the BM25 sparse encoder (Stephen Robertson & Hugo Zaragoza.)or dense vector embeddings like the BERT-based dense retriever (Karpukhin V, Oğuz B, Min S, et al.2020)) to calculate and measure the distances between vectors, thereby identifying passages or sentences relevant to the input query. text: In this section, we focus on various RAG applications tailored to different scenarios. SelfRAG effectively enhances retrieval capabilities while using fewer resources; GraphRAG performs exceptionally well when dealing with complex and extensive knowledge documents; RankRAG excels at selecting the most suitable content from numerous similar documents to pass to the LLM generation model, thereby improving output quality. 5.1 SelfRAG SelfRAG is a self-supervised version of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) model. It is a large language model capable of generating text based on given prompts or contexts. SelfRAG is trained on vast amounts of textual data from the web and employs a technique called "retrievalaugmented generation" to search for relevant information in large text corpora, incorporating this information into its generated responses. A key distinction between SelfRAG and traditional

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: relevant information in large text corpora, incorporating this information into its generated responses. A key distinction between SelfRAG and traditional RAG is that it does not rely on human feedback or reinforcement learning for training. Instead, it adopts a self-supervised learning approach, predicting whether a generated statement requires document retrieval and determining whether secondary retrieval or generation is needed based on the usefulness of the retrieved information and the relevance of the generated results to the question. This makes SelfRAG more efficient to train, more resource-efficient than other RAG frameworks, and demonstrates significant improvements in the factual accuracy and citation precision of long-form generation compared to traditional models. title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: The SelfRAG model consists of two main components: a generation model and a critique model. The generation model predicts the next token in a sequence like a conventional LLM to generate responses. The critique model determines whether retrieval is necessary and assesses the relevance and comprehensiveness of the generated content in relation to the retrieved information. During training, SelfRAG first evaluates whether the upcoming text segment requires retrieval. If not, it uses the standard LLM for generation. If retrieval is needed, it retrieves multiple pieces of content, combines them with the question, and generates the text segment in parallel. Each segment is then scored based on the relevance of the retrieved content to the question and whether the generated result is supported by the retrieved documents. The segment with the highest score is selected as the final answer. The model

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: and whether the generated result is supported by the retrieved documents. The segment with the highest score is selected as the final answer. The model learns by predicting missing words and comparing its predictions with the actual words. This self-supervised approach enables the model to learn from its mistakes and improve its response generation capabilities. To achieve this functionality, SelfRAG generates four types of reflection tokens. The "retrieve" type determines whether retrieval is needed, generating "yes" or "no" to indicate whether document retrieval is required, or "continue" to indicate that the segment can use previously retrieved content without new retrieval. The three critique tokens—IsREL, IsSUP, and IsUSE—represent whether the retrieved content is relevant to the question (relevant/irrelevant), whether the generated content is supported by the retrieved content (fully

title: RAG: The Revolution of Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
text: whether the retrieved content is relevant to the question (relevant/irrelevant), whether the generated content is supported by the retrieved content (fully supported, partially supported, no support), and the usefulness of the generated content in answering the question (rated 1–5). In summary, this framework enhances the quality and factual accuracy of generated results by incorporating reflection tokens during the LLM's prediction of the next tokens. SelfRAG is designed to handle various natural language processing tasks, such as question answering, text generation, and summarization. It can extract relevant information from vast amounts of textual data and integrate it into generated responses, producing informative and contextually relevant answers. Its self-supervised nature allows it to scale efficiently and handle large datasets, addressing the issue of context loss and making it

text: Conclusions This paper explores the working principles, architecture, and applications of RAG in the field of artificial intelligence. RAG offers numerous advantages, such as providing real-time and accurate information, enhancing the reasoning and generation capabilities of LLMs, and improving the credibility and transparency of outputs. The evolution of RAG began with strengthening the foundational knowledge of LLMs. With the emergence of conversational AI models like ChatGPT, RAG gradually became integrated into the fine-tuning and generation processes of LLMs, yielding positive results. To address the challenges of data preparation and semantic recognition in traditional RAG systems, various advanced RAG techniques have been introduced, among which SelfRAG, GraphRAG, and RankRAG are highly integrated solutions. SelfRAG is a self-supervised version of RAG particularly suitable for lightweight

GraphRAG leverages knowledge graphs to enhance the language generation process, effectively extracting and reasoning information from large volumes of text. RankRAG combines generative models with ranking models, and its data efficiency significantly reduces both data resource requirements and time costs. Future trends for RAG include improving efficiency, expanding application scope, and reducing costs—such as applying RAG to personalized responses, handling larger data volumes and user interactions, and integrating with other AI technologies.
